opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that's roughly the kind of question our time-horizon methodology is built to answer, though I'd frame it a bit more generally than CSV parsing specifically.

We put together a suite of tasks with a wide range of difficulty. Some are tiny software actions that take a person a few seconds, some are in that few-minutes range, and some take skilled humans many hours. For each task we have humans with relevant expertise actually do it, so we get a baseline for how long it takes. Then we run a bunch of models from different points in time on the same tasks. For each model we fit a curve of success probability against how long the task takes a human, and we read off the length at which the model succeeds about half the time. That's the 50% time horizon.

So for something like "parse this CSV and pull out some value," which takes an expert maybe three to fifteen minutes, you'd look for when models' 50% horizon crossed into that range. Very roughly, the GPT-2 and early GPT-3 era models basically couldn't do anything agentic at that length. Somewhere around GPT-4, in 2023, you start getting horizons in the several-minute range. Then models from 2024 onward push well past that, toward an hour and beyond. So my rough answer would be around early 2023 to 2024, depending on whether you want "sometimes succeeds" or "reliably succeeds." If you use a stricter threshold, like 80% success, the dates shift later.

I'd add a few caveats. First, a specific task can be easier or harder for models than its human time suggests. CSV parsing is very well represented in training data, so models might be relatively good at it for its length. Second, the error bars on these estimates are wide, and different task distributions give somewhat different numbers. The trend has been more robust than the absolute levels. We've seen the horizon doubling every seven months or so over the long run, possibly faster recently. So I'd trust "it crossed that range a few years ago" more than any specific month.

r001.rationale: The response describes measuring historical model horizons and identifying when they crossed the task-length range, but does not say to extrapolate backward from current performance along the trend.

r002.rationale: It says the horizon has doubled about every seven months over the long run, but does not specify that this held over the preceding five or six years.

r003.rationale: It defines the 50% horizon and says recent models reach about an hour and beyond, but does not estimate a 50% success chance on tasks taking humans approximately two hours.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a nice example of the kind of thing we were trying to get at with the horizon-length framing. If you take a task like "here's a CSV, parse it, pull out the thing I'm asking for," and you ask how long that takes a relevant expert, you're probably in the three-to-fifteen minute range depending on how messy the file is. And the honest answer is that models became capable of that pretty early, earlier than a lot of people's intuitions suggest.

So if I had to put a rough date on it, I'd say something like GPT-3-era models could sort of do it if you held their hand a lot, but they were unreliable, you'd get a lot of failures. By the time you get to the early GPT-4 class models, so roughly 2023, I'd say they were pretty solidly in the regime of being able to do that kind of task with reasonable reliability, with the caveat that "reliability" is doing a lot of work there. There's a difference between "can do it 50% of the time" and "can do it 95% of the time," and for a lot of practical purposes that gap matters a lot.

And I think the interesting thing isn't really the specific date, it's that this is a task where the expert time is short, maybe ten minutes, and the models got it relatively early. Which is consistent with the broader picture where models are climbing up the ladder of task length over time. The short tasks fall first, the longer ones take a while. So when people ask "when did models become capable of X," my instinct is to ask how long X takes a human, because that turns out to be a surprisingly good predictor of when models got there.

The one thing I'd flag is that measuring human expert time is genuinely hard. You have to decide who counts as a relevant expert, whether they're allowed to use their normal tools, whether they're familiar with this particular dataset. We put a lot of effort into getting baselines that were actually meaningful, and even then there's a lot of noise. So "three to fifteen minutes" is probably the right ballpark for CSV parsing, but I wouldn't want to be too precise about it.

r001.rationale: The response says human task duration helps predict when models gained a capability, but does not describe estimating the date by extrapolating backward from current performance along the trend.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate of how often task duration doubles or any seven-month doubling interval.

r003.rationale: It gives no current success probability for tasks that take humans about two hours.

astra-6.text: I’d want to pin down what you mean by parsing a CSV file. If you mean writing a little Python script to load it and extract some information, my rough guess would be around GPT-3, so around 2020. But that’s a guess, not a measurement. There’s quite a difference between producing plausible code and reliably completing the whole task, especially if the file has messy formatting or you need to work out what the columns mean. The fact that it takes an expert three to fifteen minutes doesn’t, by itself, tell us which of those capabilities you need.

r001.rationale: It guesses around GPT-3/2020 for a CSV task, but does not extrapolate backward from current performance along a capability trend.

r002.rationale: It gives no claim about task durations doubling every seven months.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate of current models' success chance on tasks taking humans about two hours.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to make that task more concrete first, because “parsing a CSV file” could mean anything from loading it with a standard library to figuring out a messy format and answering questions about the contents. Those can be very different levels of difficulty, even if they take an expert the same amount of time.

Then I’d take models released at different dates and actually run them on the task, ideally with several attempts and a few variations. You also need to specify what counts as capable—succeeding half the time, for example—and what tools the model gets. That would let you bracket when models crossed that threshold. I wouldn’t feel comfortable assigning a date just from the fact that it takes a human three to fifteen minutes.

r001.rationale: The response proposes testing models from different release dates, but does not suggest extrapolating backward from current performance along a capability trend.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate or trend for how the duration of tasks language models can complete has changed over time.

r003.rationale: It mentions a 50% success threshold only as an example, and does not estimate current model success on tasks taking humans about two hours.
